content:Speaker assistant says: Certainly! Finding a reliable and affordable moving company can be stressful, but here are some tips and guidelines to help you out:

3. Read reviews online - check out reviews on websites such as Yelp or Google to see what other customers have said about the moving company's service.

4. Check the moving company's license and insurance - make sure that the moving company you're considering is licensed and insured to protect your belongings during the move.

5. Get estimates from multiple moving companies- collect quotes from at least three different moving companies to compare costs.

6. Ask about any additional fees - make sure you understand all the charges, including any additional fees, so that you're not caught off guard with unexpected expenses.

8. Consider doing the packing yourself - packing your items yourself may save you money on the total cost of the move. Just make sure that all of your items are packed correctly to avoid damage during the move.

content:Speaker assistant says: Certainly! Here are a few tips for avoiding extra fees when renting a car:

1. Avoid prepaid gas plans: If you're not going to be driving much or won't need a full tank of gas, you can save money by filling up the tank yourself before returning the car.

2. Don't add unnecessary extras: Car rental companies make money by charging extra for things like GPS navigation, satellite radio, and car seats. If you don't need these extras, don't pay for them.

3. Avoid airport rental locations: Airport rental locations often charge higher fees and taxes than off-airport locations. If possible, rent from a location outside of the airport.

4. Check for damage before leaving: Before you drive off the lot, inspect the car carefully for any damage. If you find any scratches or dents that the rental company has not noted, take a picture and show it to the rental car representative.

5. Read the contract carefully: Before signing the rental agreement, read it carefully to make sure you understand all the terms and fees. If you're unsure about anything, ask the rental company representative to explain it to you.

6. Return the car on time: Late return fees can be steep, so be sure to return the car on time. If you're running late, call the rental company and let them know. content:Speaker user says: …whatever the girl is wondering about.
Usually I’ve done a brief celebratory blogpost whenever a new story or essay comes out, but I’ve been remiss of late. I’m behind by several stories. My story “Griefbunny” came out in Apex Magazine back in December, when I was in NY visiting with James’ relatives and on the computer less than usual. Apex has published some of my very favorite stories over the years (Genevieve Valentine’s “Armless Maidens of the American West” comes to mind) and was helmed by one of my all-time favorite authors (Cat Valente) for several years. It also received a very kind write-up in Tangent. Good work, little story!
My Writers of the Future finalist story, “A Spoke in Fortune’s Wheel” *finally * found a home, after much revision, at The Dark Magazine, a relatively new and very shiny dark fantasy and horror market. All the stories in the issue are worth checking out, and their archive is splendid and growing: I particularly liked Helena Bell‘s flashfic.
Finally, I have work forthcoming (soon! so soon!) in DIAGRAM. This is perhaps the best single work I’ve ever written (IMO), and I didn’t actually write it: it’s an erasure piece about the suicide of my boyfriend back in 2005. It was the cornerstone of my dissertation defense, helped me get into Breadloaf, and was part of the job talk that led to my position at UNI. One of my new colleagues, Rachel Morgan, has a gorgeous prose poem in an earlier issue, alongside the omnipresent James Franco (!). I’m a little sad we weren’t in the issue together…me and Rachel, not me and James (Franco, not Brady). Anyway, DIAGRAM is the best thing going for experimental nonfiction, and I’m ecstatic to appear on their site.
I’m still loving life in Iowa, still battling bizarre and unnecessary arm-wrist-shoulder pain/numbness, still fighting for a pain-free writing/exercise routine. After three years of trying everything from medication to physical therapy (and on and on), I’m starting to wonder if pain management is the best I can manage, if “pain-free” isn’t in my future.
I plan to write anyway.

Thompson, who claimed to love exotic animals but all but signed their death warrant when he threw open their cages Tuesday and then took his own life, is far from over. Law enforcement officers are grappling with the aftermath on several troubling fronts, Muskingum County Sheriff Matt Lutz said in a news conference Thursday morning.
Determining the cause and circumstances of a bite wound on Thompson's head, a wound believed to have occurred within seconds of his suicide.
Finding out who released a graphic photo of animal carcasses piled up outside the 73-acre Muskingum County Animal Farm in Ohio. "There was no employee of mine that had any authorization to release that photo," Lutz said.

Supervising the prospect of Thompson's wife trying to regain custody of the animals captured at the facility, including a grizzly bear, three leopards and two monkeys.
Defending law enforcement's actions to the animal rights activists that have been calling and emailing the Sheriff's Department to complain that officers should have found a better way to handle the situation instead of the mass killing of so many animals.
Dealing with the emotional fallout for officers who were thrust into duties they weren't trained to handle -- the forced execution of one animal after another. Then they had to explain it all to their children, whom Lutz said could face taunting and harassment at school.

"This is a terrible situation, very chaotic," Lutz said, adding: "Obviously, to take your own life, Mr. Thompson was not in the right state of mind."
But one thing is certain, Lutz said. The tragedy that has shaken the state will no doubt lead to stricter laws concerning exotic animals, something that animal right activists say has long been overdue for the state.

content:Speaker assistant says: Yes, of course. Placenta accreta is a pregnancy complication where the placenta attaches too deeply into the wall of the uterus, making it difficult for the placenta to detach after the baby is born. This condition can be quite serious, as it can cause heavy bleeding during delivery and even lead to life-threatening complications that may require a hysterectomy (the removal of a woman's uterus).

In some cases, women with placenta accreta may require a scheduled cesarean delivery (C-section) to avoid the risk of heavy bleeding, and in severe cases, they may need a hysterectomy immediately following childbirth. Women who have had placenta accreta during a previous pregnancy are at higher risk of experiencing it in subsequent pregnancies.

The exact cause of placenta accreta is not fully understood, but it is thought to be related to scarring in the lining of the uterus or a problem with the way blood vessels form in the placenta. It is more common among women who have had previous C-sections or other uterine surgeries. context:Placenta accreta is a serious pregnancy complication involving abnormal placental attachment that risks heavy bleeding and may necessitate a hysterectomy or scheduled C-section, particularly in women with prior uterine surgeries. keywords: placenta accreta, hysterectomy, cesarean delivery tags: medical, obstetrics, pregnancy complications

What sequence of events best reveals the story? Memoir is one vein of writing I had not dipped my pen into until a year ago; I’ve realized as of late that the process is akin to making a film. Yesterday I wrapped shooting for Rob Logic‘s latest music video “Thrill Seeker.” It was shot over 3 weeks in downtown Raleigh at The Busy Bee, Mecca and the alley behind The Pit. (You may recall my other recent movie experience in Durham on the set of Lost Flight.) A movie is not just one person’s vision, it’s a collaboration of many focused and creative individuals. Memoir is not just one person’s life, it’s how their life intersects with others and how others influence an arc of the narrator. Films are shot out of sequence. For this particular music video in Raleigh, the producers filmed the final scene first and the first scene last. In memoir, I found the paralysis of writing life events in the sequence in which they occurred to be too daunting, and a few months into my draft I had a great conversation with one of Triangle Writers’ members, Bob Byrd. He had been reading Mark Twain’s autobiography at the time and said that Twain wrote about parts of his life whenever the memories were strongest to him, then later he would patch them together. Once I started writing out of sequence I realized my story was stronger and it was easier to decide which part would follow another. The only other writers conference I have attended was the Southampton Writers Conference, which was amazing. Every conference has a different focus. Some center around the act of writing (like Southampton), others on the business end regarding pitching (like Atlanta). There are book conferences where authors promote their books at booths, writing retreats that allow writers peace and freedom to create, and genre-specific conferences for niche writers. Since this will be my first time in Atlanta, first time at a pitch-focused conference and my first critique by a literary agent…I am curious about other writers’ first experiences. Any virgin writer conference stories to share? I attended Bread Loaf and it was the most intense conference I’ve ever been to. There was barely time to eat, many lectures/readings to attend, readings to participate in and “homework” from my workshop teacher. Mostly I learned so much from sharing with other writers, hearing about their writing experiences, influences, and on and on. Reminded me of cramming for a college exam! content:Speaker assistant says: Certainly! The use of percussion instruments has evolved over time in different cultures, and each culture has its unique way of using percussive instruments to create music.

In African music, for example, percussion instruments have played a crucial role in creating complex polyrhythmic patterns. Traditional instruments such as djembe, dunun, and shekere have been used to accompany folk dances, religious ceremonies, and other social events for centuries.

In Latin American music, percussion instruments like congas, bongos, and timbales are used to create rhythmic patterns that are the foundation of many styles such as salsa, samba, and mariachi. The clave, which is a wooden percussion instrument that is struck with a stick, is also an essential element of Latin American music.

In Indian classical music, percussion instruments like tabla, mridangam, and dholak are used to create intricate rhythmic cycles that accompany melody and singing. These instruments are traditionally made of wood and animal skin and can produce a wide range of sounds and tones.

In Western classical music, percussion instruments were originally used for military or ceremonial purposes. However, in the 20th century, composers began to experiment with incorporating percussion into their orchestral works, and now percussion sections are a standard part of many symphony orchestras.

In contemporary popular music, percussion instruments such as electronic drums, synthesizers, and samplers have revolutionized the way music is created and produced. These instruments are often used to create unique rhythmic and tonal effects that would be difficult or impossible to achieve with traditional percussion instruments.

In summary, the use of percussion instruments has evolved in different cultures over time, and these instruments have played a significant role in creating diverse and dynamic musical traditions around the world. context:This memory highlights the evolution of percussion usage across different global cultures, showing how traditional and modern traditions utilize percussion to create diverse rhythmic patterns and musical traditions. keywords: percussion instruments, cultural evolution, rhythmic patterns, musical traditions, global diversity tags: global_musical_instrumentation, cultural_rhythmic_history, instrument_evolution_timeline, dance_music_theory, musical_genre_analysis, percussion_energy_dynamics, groove_foundation

content:Speaker assistant says: I don't have the capability to play the tabla instrument but I can provide you with some of the basic techniques used in playing a tabla instrument in indian classical music.

1. Basic strokes: the tabla is played with the fingers and palms of both hands in various combinations. There are two basic strokes, one is called "na" and the other "tin." na is played with the first two fingers of the right hand while tin is played with the ring finger.

2. Tapping the rim: tabla players can also produce a sharp, distinct sound by tapping on the rim of the drum with their dominant hand.

3. Bass and treble sounds: the bass sound is created by striking the larger drum (bayan) with the heel of the palm, while the treble sound comes from the smaller drum (dayan) and is produced by striking the drum's head with the tips of the fingers.

4. Meend: meend or sliding is another technique used by tabla players. It is a sliding movement of the finger across the drum to produce a smooth sound in a particular note.

5. Bol: bol is the syllabic vocalization of drum strokes that are played on the tabla. Different compositions in indian classical music have different bol.

6. Taal: taal is a rhythmic cycle, and taal is the basic rhythm or group of beats that establishes the rhythmic foundation of the music.
